How is New Hampshire organized when you sell a house here?

New Hampshire is divided into 10 counties, and the state is split into 234 municipalities, made up of 221 towns and 13 cities. Under state law, cities and towns are treated the same, so a house in a small town follows the same basic rules as one in Manchester.

That split matters because the work of selling a house is shared between two levels of government. The town or city assesses and bills property tax. The county runs the registry of deeds, where your deed is recorded, and the probate court sits in each of the ten counties.

Population is uneven. Hillsborough County has 433,415 residents and holds both Manchester and Nashua as county seats. Coös County has 31,343. We buy houses across the state, and you can browse by place on this page, including Manchester, Concord and Dover.

How does the transfer tax work when you sell a house in New Hampshire?

New Hampshire charges a real estate transfer tax of $0.75 per $100 of the sale price, and the Department of Revenue Administration says the tax is imposed on both the buyer and the seller. In practical terms, each side owes its own share, so a seller should expect a line for it on the closing statement.

The statute rounds up fractional hundreds and sets a $20 minimum when the price is $4,000 or less. To see how it scales, here is the math on three prices, for one party.

Sale priceTax for one party at $0.75 per $100
$250,000$1,875
$400,000$3,000
$600,000$4,500

The law also lists exemptions, which turn on the facts, so ask your closing attorney or the Department of Revenue Administration. For the filing side, see our guide to recording a deed in New Hampshire.

Who do you call about property taxes and recording?

Call the town or city tax collector for a bill, and the county registry of deeds for a recorded document. Each of the ten counties keeps its own registry, and state law makes the register of deeds responsible for keeping the county records safe and in the county office.

The property tax year runs from April 1 to March 31, and taxes are assessed on the inventory taken in April. Municipalities that adopt semi-annual billing send a first bill that is due July 1 and a second for the remainder that is due December 1. Ask the collector for a current payoff figure early.

If you think the assessment is too high, an abatement application goes to the selectmen or assessors in writing by March 1 following the notice of tax. The board must grant or deny it by July 1, and no answer counts as a denial. Our New Hampshire property tax guide walks through appeals and exemptions, and we have local office details for Manchester, Nashua and Concord.

  • Tax bills and payoff amounts: your town or city tax collector
  • Assessment questions: your selectmen or assessors
  • Deed recording and copies: your county registry of deeds

How does foreclosure work in New Hampshire?

New Hampshire lenders can foreclose without going to court by using a power of sale clause in the mortgage, so a foreclosure here can move faster than in states that require a lawsuit. The rules sit in RSA 479:25.

For the sale to be valid, the lender must follow several steps.

  • Publish notice once a week for three weeks in a newspaper of general circulation, with the first notice at least 20 days before the sale.
  • Serve or mail the owner a copy of the notice at least 25 days before the sale, or at least 45 days before for a residential mortgage.
  • Include the right to petition the superior court to stop the sale, and for owner-occupied homes of four units or fewer, the state banking department hotline information.

An owner who wants to challenge the notice or the sale has to act quickly. A court petition must be filed and served before the sale, and claims over the form of notice or the conduct of the sale are cut off one year and one day after the foreclosure deed is recorded. If you have received a notice, talk to an attorney or the banking department hotline first.

What should heirs know before selling an inherited house?

Start with the probate court. New Hampshire's Circuit Court Probate Division handles wills, trusts and estates, and it holds sessions from courthouses in each of the ten counties. In contested matters it offers mediation with probate trained mediators at no charge to the parties.

Timing depends on the court and on whether anyone disputes the will, so we give no number of weeks here. Our guides on the probate process and the estate and inheritance tax cover what heirs usually need to gather. The court's toll free line is 1-855-212-1234 from the US or Canada.

Does the homestead right affect a sale?

The homestead right protects a home from certain creditors, and it does not reduce your tax bill. RSA 480:1 entitles every person to $400,000 of value in their homestead, and the statute says exemptions held by a household total no more than $550,000. The current amount took effect on January 1, 2026.

To claim it, you must have used the residence as your primary home for the previous 12 months. Proceeds from selling a qualifying home are also protected if reinvested in a new primary residence within 6 months. Do not confuse it with local property tax exemptions, which are a separate topic covered in our homestead exemption guide.

What if the house has tenants?

A sale does not remove a tenant, so plan for the tenancy before you list. Under RSA 540:3, residential tenants get 30 days' notice in all cases, except that 7 days is enough when the reason is nonpayment of rent, substantial damage, behavior that threatens health or safety, or the domestic violence provision.

For what the statute calls restricted property, a landlord can end a tenancy only for listed reasons, including unpaid rent, damage, a material lease breach and other good cause. For a lease of 12 months or longer, the lease can end at its expiration if the landlord gave written notice at least 60 days ahead and files a possessory action within 6 months. The notice has to state the reason with specificity.

Because the rules vary with the property and lease, read our guides to eviction notices, the eviction process and landlord and tenant law before you act. We can also buy a house with tenants in place.

What does an as-is cash sale mean in New Hampshire?

It means the buyer takes the house in its current condition and you skip repairs, staging and open houses. It does not mean you skip disclosure or paperwork.

New Hampshire requires the seller or seller's agent to give the buyer a written notice before the purchase contract is signed, and the buyer signs to acknowledge it. The notice covers radon, arsenic, lead, PFAS and flood risk. The statute adds that failing to give it does not affect the validity of the title transferred. Nearly half of the state's residents rely on a private well, and the Department of Environmental Services says arsenic and radon occur naturally in the rock and soil, so a well and its test results are worth gathering early.

  • Pre-1978 homes may have lead paint.
  • Coastal and waterfront homes may face flood risk that standard homeowners insurance typically does not cover.
  • PFAS shows up more often in southern New Hampshire wells.

Ask whichever title company or attorney handles your closing how they work, since practice varies.

Frequently asked questions

How many counties does New Hampshire have?

Ten. Hillsborough is the largest at 433,415 people, and Coös is the smallest at 31,343. Each county has its own registry of deeds and a probate court location.

How much is the New Hampshire transfer tax?

The rate is $0.75 per $100 of the price, and it is imposed on both the buyer and the seller. Your closing statement will show the exact figure.

Can a lender foreclose without a court case in New Hampshire?

Yes, through a power of sale in the mortgage under RSA 479:25. The owner of a residential mortgage must receive notice at least 45 days before the sale.

How much does the homestead right protect?

$400,000 per person as of January 1, 2026, with household totals capped at $550,000. You must have lived in the home as your primary residence for the previous 12 months.

What notice must a landlord give a tenant?

Thirty days for residential tenancies, or 7 days for reasons such as nonpayment of rent or damage. The notice must state the reason with specificity.

Do I have to give disclosures about radon and well water?

Sellers or their agents must hand the buyer a notice covering radon, arsenic, lead, PFAS and flood before the contract is signed. The buyer signs to confirm receipt.

Where do I record a deed after a sale?

At the registry of deeds in the county where the property sits. Ask the office or your closing agent about fees and format.
